lines: Five identical, healthy nodes each get a real, deterministic timeout.
The one whose timeout fires first becomes a candidate and asks for votes. Does it genuinely win, and does the winner genuinely match the fastest timeout?
answer: The fastest real timeout genuinely wins.

lines: Run it for real: the election genuinely elects the node whose real timeout fired first, with a real majority of votes.
Now one candidate's own log is genuinely behind the rest of the cluster's.
Does its vote request still win, or does the up-to-date-log voting rule genuinely reject it?
answer: A fresh term alone was never enough.

lines: Run it for real: the out-of-date candidate's own vote request is genuinely rejected, by the real up-to-date-log voting rule; it loses the election.
steps.takeaway: A fresh term alone is never enough; the voting rule also checks whether a log is genuinely caught up.

lines: A healthy cluster has a live leader. One node gets partitioned and, missing every heartbeat, keeps incrementing its own term locally.
When it rejoins and broadcasts that stale, inflated term, does the healthy leader genuinely step down?
answer: Every node updates to a higher term it sees.

lines: Run it for real: genuinely disruptive. Every node updates its own term the moment it sees a higher one, and the healthy leader genuinely steps down.
steps.takeaway: A bare term increase alone, with nothing else genuinely wrong, can depose a working leader.

lines: Now the identical partitioned node runs a real pre-vote round first, before ever raising its own term.
Does pre-voting genuinely stop the identical disruption this time?

Run it for real: with that pre-vote round, every healthy voter already has a live leader and genuinely denies it; the partitioned node's own term never rises, and the healthy leader is never disturbed.
steps.takeaway: Pre-voting protects a leader before any real term is ever spent trying to depose it.

lines: One real, widely used consensus implementation's own documentation states this exact purpose directly, in its own words.
It names stopping a partitioned node from disrupting the cluster on rejoin, directly.
So here's the real shape of this whole topic: timing alone picks a candidate, but two separate guardrails decide whether that pick is actually safe.
One guardrail looks backward, at whether a candidate's own history is caught up; the other looks forward, refusing to even spend a higher term until winning is already likely.
Neither guardrail needs a clock anyone trusts, or a human watching; both come straight out of comparing plain numbers a node already has on hand.
